subject: Climate & Environment
title: The High Seas Treaty
description: A micro-lesson that makes The High Seas Treaty usable.

hook.text: Two-thirds of the ocean belongs to no country. Until 2023, there was no way to protect it.

buildup.text: The high seas — beyond 200 nautical miles from any coast — lacked any conservation framework.

discovery.text: The UN High Seas Treaty allows creation of marine protected areas in international waters for the first time.

twist.text: Negotiations took nearly 20 years. Deep-sea mining interests and fishing lobbies fought every clause.

climax.text: The treaty must still be ratified and enforced — the hardest part of any international agreement.

punchline.text: The largest wild space on Earth finally has a set of rules.

quiz.question: What does the UN High Seas Treaty enable?
options: Creating marine protected areas in international waters
Banning all fishing in the ocean

details.summary: The High Seas Treaty, adopted in 2023 after two decades of negotiation, creates a legal framework for establishing marine protected areas in international waters beyond national jurisdiction. It covers nearly two-thirds of the ocean that previously had minimal environmental governance.
details.whyItMatters: Without the treaty, the vast majority of the ocean had no mechanism for conservation. It is a landmark step toward the global goal of protecting 30 percent of the ocean by 2030.
takeaways: The treaty covers international waters beyond national zones
It enables marine protected areas on the high seas for the first time
Negotiations took over 20 years to complete

faq.question: What are the high seas?
faq.answer: The high seas are ocean areas beyond any country's 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone. They cover about 64 percent of the ocean surface and nearly half of Earth's total area. Until this treaty, they were largely unregulated for conservation.

faq.question: When will the treaty take effect?
faq.answer: The treaty needs ratification by 60 countries before entering into force. As of early 2025, many nations have signed but ratification is progressing slowly. Full implementation will require funding, monitoring infrastructure, and enforcement mechanisms.
